title: Fast-evolving human regions (HAQERs) carry an old human-specific excess of fixed changes beyond shared mutation hotspots, but published divergence-polymorphism tests cannot attribute it to selection
abstract: Human ancestor quickly evolved regions (HAQERs) combine a mutation hotspot shared with chimpanzees and an extra human-specific excess of old, fixed changes; the published polymorphism tests cannot show that positive selection made that excess, because an old neutral burst that has stopped explains it as well. This matters because HAQERs are described as new brain enhancers that positive selection made from neutral DNA. HAQERs are 500-bp windows with the most changes between the human-chimpanzee ancestor and humans. We counted human- and chimpanzee-lineage substitutions (ancestor from gorilla and orangutan) and gnomAD v4.1 variants (76,215 genomes) in 1,479 Gapped and 1,167 Consensus HAQERs, their flanks, 20,000 random windows and placebo windows selected only for fast chimpanzee change. In well-called Gapped HAQER DNA, human-lineage divergence was 5.4 times the random rate, chimpanzee-lineage divergence 2.1 times and human polymorphism 1.8 times, so polymorphism followed the shared hotspot. The human lineage had 2.6 times (95% CI 2.4-2.9) more change than the chimpanzee lineage, or about 1.4-2.1 times after correction for window selection on noisy counts, which inflated rates 1.15-2.2 times in held-out halves. Divergence divided by polymorphism, a published sign of selection, is therefore inflated by an amount that cannot be measured for the published calls; in clean HAQERs it only restates the human-specific excess. The share of divergent sites still polymorphic in humans, a second published sign, was 0.62 of the random value (7.6% vs 12.2%), 0.65 (0.58-0.72) after matching for duplications, repeats and poor variant calls, 0.71 with failed calls counted, and 0.55 in clean sites; flanks and placebo windows showed no deficit. Within HAQERs this share fell from 1.12 to 0.44 of random as the human-specific excess rose, so both signs describe one old excess. The Consensus set is not a clean replication: a screen that counts only fixed differences gave 0.36-0.42 even in random DNA. In clean HAQERs, the excess of A/T to G/C changes rose with recombination (ratio up to 2.1-2.8; random 0.9), a sign of GC-biased gene conversion, but the deficit of polymorphic sites occurred in all substitution classes. Limits: chimpanzee polymorphism data and a divergence-matched null are needed to separate selection from an extinct recombination hot spot or other ended burst.

display.caption: A: human-lineage divergence, chimpanzee-lineage divergence and human polymorphism relative to random DNA (95% bootstrap intervals), for all and for well-called (clean) HAQER DNA. In clean DNA, polymorphism follows the chimpanzee rate (a shared hotspot) and the human lineage has an extra excess. B: divergence divided by polymorphism, the published sign of selection; filled bars show the lineage used to select the windows (the placebo value falls to about 1.25 on held-out halves). C: winner's curse: rate in the half of each window used for selection divided by the rate in the held-out half.

Share of divergent sites still polymorphic in humans, relative to random DNA. Below 1 means more fixed sites, the published sign of selection. The deficit in HAQERs stays after matching for duplications, repeats and poor calls, with or without failed variant calls, and in clean sites; flanks and placebo windows show none.

A: A/T to G/C over G/C to A/T for clean human-lineage changes by local recombination tertile; the rise in HAQERs is the sign of GC-biased gene conversion. B: within HAQERs, the polymorphic share of divergent sites falls as the human-specific excess (D_h/D_c) rises; diamonds show the value expected if the whole excess were fixed.
